{"idea":{"Name":"coarsening_shear_memory","Title":"Does Shear Remember the Coarsening Path? A Conditional Test of Memory in Mechatronic Time Crystallization","Short Hypothesis":"The source study reports spatial coarsening; this follow-up asks whether mean shear magnitude is determined by the instantaneous correlation width or also depends on the width’s recent trajectory. In the supplied aggregate, width rises overall while shear is elevated early and later settles into a narrower range, making a lagged, path-dependent relation a testable hypothesis, not an established result. The key test is whether shear differs at matched widths when width is growing versus shrinking, after accounting for serial dependence and time trends.","Related Work":"The visible source, “Wave coarsening drives time crystallization in mechatronic metamaterials,” reports coarsening in this system. The proposed analysis does not claim to rediscover coarsening or establish a new material mechanism; it tests a distinct conditional question about hysteresis or memory between coarsening and shear. The supplied corpus is the only literature context available here, so novelty relative to other literature remains unresolved.","Abstract":"Spatial coarsening is an established conclusion of the source study. A distinct follow-up question is whether the shear observable tracks the instantaneous spatial correlation width, or retains information about the recent coarsening path. We hypothesize conditionally that, at the same width, mean shear may differ depending on whether width has recently been increasing or decreasing. This would be consistent with a lagged response or hysteresis, but could also arise from a shared time trend, smoothing, or measurement noise. We will analyze only the supplied 2,199-sample experimental aggregate, treating samples as a serial time series rather than independent replicates. After checking sampling regularity and plotting both observables, we will compare a baseline smooth model of shear from width and time against a model that additionally includes a prespecified lagged width change and its interaction with width-growth direction. We will test robustness across reasonable smoothing windows and lag choices, using blocked time-series validation and block-bootstrap uncertainty rather than row-wise random splits. The conditional prediction is that the lag term improves held-out prediction and the estimated shear difference between growth and decline remains directionally stable at matched widths. If this pattern vanishes after controlling for time or is unstable to analysis choices, the memory hypothesis is unsupported by this export. Even a robust association would motivate, not prove, a dynamical mechanism: the aggregate lacks repeated-run identifiers, raw image sequences, and independently characterized uncertainty. The result would be a careful hypothesis-generating test and a concrete specification for future controlled experiments.","Experiments":["Load measurements.csv, verify columns, row count, time ordering, missing values, and duplicate timestamps. Plot time series and scatterplots of width and shear. Exclude or explicitly flag zero-width rows if present; do not use the inverse-width column where width is zero.","Fit a baseline smooth regression predicting mean_shear_magnitude from correlation_width and time using low-complexity splines. Fit an augmented model adding lagged width change over a prespecified primary window (for example, 0.1 s), plus an interaction with the sign of that change. Standardize predictors; compare nested models using blocked contiguous time-series folds, not random splits.","Estimate the matched-width growth-versus-decline shear contrast only where increasing and decreasing segments have overlapping width ranges. Report its sign, magnitude, uncertainty, and effective time coverage; avoid extrapolating across non-overlap.","Assess uncertainty with a moving-block bootstrap over contiguous samples, with block sizes chosen to cover plausible autocorrelation scales estimated from residuals. Treat results as descriptive for this single aggregate, not as replication-level inference.","Run sensitivity checks across a small, declared set of lag windows and smoothness settings, and compare against time-only and width-only baselines. Report held-out RMSE and MAE, residual autocorrelation, and whether the directional contrast is stable. Do not select and report only the best lag."] ,"Risk Factors and Limitations":"This is one exported aggregate, not independent experimental runs; serial samples cannot establish population-level significance. Width and shear may share time trends, and unreported aggregation or smoothing may create apparent lag or hysteresis. The exported standard-error column lacks documented independence and aggregation details, so it cannot support conventional replicate-level uncertainty. Growth and decline may not overlap sufficiently in width for a fair matched comparison. Results could be sensitive to lag and smoothing choices, and no causal mechanism can be inferred without raw trajectories or controlled perturbations. External literature novelty is unresolved because external search was disabled."}}
